# Problem 1
```{r, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(p8105.datasets)
library(tidyverse)

data("ny_noaa")

ny_noaa
```
We want to know the size and the structure of the data.

## Overview of the data
```{r}
dim(ny_noaa)
glimpse(ny_noaa)
summary(ny_noaa)

ny_noaa |>
  summarise(
    total_rows = n(),
    total_stations = n_distinct(id),
    missing_date = sum(is.na(date)),
    missing_prcp = sum(is.na(prcp)),
    missing_snow = sum(is.na(snow)),
    missing_snwd = sum(is.na(snwd)),
    missing_tmax = sum(is.na(tmax)),
    missing_tmin = sum(is.na(tmin))
  )
```
**A short description based on the data:**
The `ny_noaa` dataset contains daily weather observations from `r scales::comma(nrow(ny_noaa))` records across `r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` weather stations in New York State. It has `r ncol(ny_noaa)` variables, including station ID (`id`), observation date (`date`), precipitation (`prcp`), snowfall (`snow`), snow depth (`snwd`), maximum temperature (`tmax`), and minimum temperature (`tmin`). The observations span from 1981 to 2010. Missing data are an important issue. Precipitation has 145,838 missing values, snowfall has 381,221, and snow depth has 591,786. The temperature variables (tmax and tmin) are stored as character variables, and their missing values should also be examined.

## Data Cleaning
```{r}
noaa_df =
  ny_noaa |>
  janitor::clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year = as.numeric(str_sub(date, 1, 4)),
    month = as.numeric(str_sub(date, 6, 7)),
    day = as.numeric(str_sub(date, 9, 10)),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = as.numeric(prcp) / 10,
    snow = as.numeric(snow),
    snwd = as.numeric(snwd)
  )
```

Snow falls
```{r}
noaa_df |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10)
```
The most commonly observed snowfall value is expected to be 0 mm because snowfall does not occur on most observation days. 

## Average max temperature in January and in July
```{r, warning=FALSE}
temp_df =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(
    mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    month = factor(
      month,
      levels = c(1, 7),
      labels = c("January", "July")
    )
  )

ggplot(
  temp_df,
  aes(
    x = year,
    y = mean_tmax,
    group = id
  )
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.15, color = "blue") +
  facet_grid(. ~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in January and July",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Average Maximum Temperature (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 14, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 9),
    strip.text = element_text(size = 11)
  )
```


**Summary of the plots:**
July has much higher average maximum temperatures (mostly around 25–30°C) than January (mostly around −5–5°C). There is variation among stations in both months, shown by the many overlapping lines. January temperatures appear more variable than July temperatures. There is no obvious long-term increasing or decreasing trend in either panel. Temperatures fluctuate from year to year.

Potential outliers: A few stations show unusually low values. In July, some observations fall well below the main cluster, including one in the late 1980s. In January, a few observations fall below −10°C. 


## tmax vs tmin for the full dataset
```{r}
p_temp =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(tmax), !is.na(tmin)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 50) +
  labs(
    title = "Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Minimum Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Maximum Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```


## Distribution of snowfall values greater than 0 and less than 100
```{r}
p_snow =
  noaa_df |>
  filter(!is.na(snow), snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_violin(
    fill = "lightblue",
    color = "gray",
    alpha = 0.8,
    scale = "width",
    width = 0.9,
    trim = TRUE
  ) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = seq(1981, 2010, by = 2)) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall Distribution by Year",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(size = 12, face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 8, angle = 45, hjust = 1)
  )
```

```{r, fig.width=14, fig.height=6}
library(patchwork)
p_temp + p_snow +
  plot_layout(widths = c(1, 1.5))
```


**Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature:** The plot shows a positive association between minimum and maximum temperatures. Days with higher minimum temperatures generally also have higher maximum temperatures. Most observations are concentrated in the central region, while a few extreme values appear to be potential outliers.

**Snowfall Distribution by Year:** The snowfall distributions appear similar across years, with multiple peaks around certain snowfall amounts. The distributions are spread across a wide range of snowfall amounts. Overall, there is no obvious change in the snowfall distribution over time.

# Problem 2
## Load, tidy, and merge the dataset
```{r, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(knitr)

covar =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_covar.csv", 
    skip = 4,
    col_names = TRUE,
    na = c("", ".", "NA")) |>
  clean_names()

accel =
  read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv", na = c("", ".", "NA"))|>
  clean_names()

covar_tidy <- covar |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(
      education, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school"))
  ) |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  drop_na()         

nhanes_wide <- inner_join(covar_tidy, accel, by = "seqn") |>
  mutate(seqn = as.character(seqn))     

nhanes_long <- nhanes_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute", names_prefix = "min", values_to = "mims") |>
  mutate(minute = as.integer(minute))

dim(nhanes_wide) 
```

```{r}
nhanes_covar_clean =
  covar |>
  filter(
    age >= 21,
    !is.na(age),
    !is.na(sex),
    !is.na(education)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(
      sex,
      levels = c(1, 2),
      labels = c("Male", "Female")
    ),
    education = factor(
      education,
      levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c(
        "Less than high school",
        "High school equivalent",
        "More than high school"
      ),
      ordered = TRUE
    )
  )
```

## Table for the number of men and women in each education category
```{r}
nhanes_wide |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n, values_fill = 0) |>
  kable(caption = "Number of men and women in each education category",
        col.names = c("Education", "Men", "Women"))
```
**Comments on table:**
Men and women are almost evenly split in the "less than high school" group and in the "more than high school" group. The "high school equivalent" group has more men than women. The "more than high school" group is by far the largest, with 115 of the 228 participants, about half of the sample. The other two groups are small, so comparisons within them should be read with caution.


## Age distributions for men and women in each education category
```{r}
nhanes_wide |>
  ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(title = "Age distribution by sex and education",
       x = "Sex", y = "Age (years)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
```

**Comments on visualization:**
Median age is highest in the "less than high school" group and lowest in the "more than high school" group. So the more educated participants tend to be younger. Older cohorts in the US generally completed less schooling, so age and education are confounded. The sexes look similar in the first and third groups, with nearly identical medians and spreads.  In the "high school equivalent" group, Women are older, and the women's middle 50% sits higher. There are only 23 women in that group, this gap could be partly due to chance. Across all groups the ages span roughly 21 to 80, so each group includes both young and old adults. The boxplots show the spread, but they don't show the sample sizes, so they should be read together with the table.


## Total Activity
```{r}
nhanes_wide <- nhanes_wide |>
  mutate(total_activity = rowSums(across(starts_with("min"))))

nhanes_wide |>
  ggplot(aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(title = "Total daily activity versus age",
       x = "Age (years)", y = "Total MIMS over 24 hours", color = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```
**Total activity versus age：**
Total activity falls with age in all three education groups, from roughly 14,000 to 18,000 MIMS in the twenties and thirties to about 9,000 to 10,000 by age 80. The decline is steepest and most consistent in the "less than high school" group. Men and women track each other closely. In the "high school equivalent" group, women are clearly more active than men until about age 60. The two sexes then converge at older ages. In the "more than high school" group, activity is fairly flat until about 60 and then declines. Women stay slightly above men at most ages. Overall, women are at or above men in some places, but the gap is small compared with the scatter between individuals. The smooth curves are wiggly in the smaller groups, so differences there should not be over-interpreted.


## 24 hour time courses
```{r}
nhanes_long |>
  ggplot(aes(x = minute / 60, y = mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(aes(group = seqn), alpha = 0.05) +
  geom_smooth(aes(group = sex), se = FALSE, linewidth = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ education, ncol = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 24, 4)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 75)) +
  labs(title = "24-hour activity profiles by education and sex",
       x = "Hour of day (0 = midnight)", y = "MIMS", color = "Sex") +
  theme_minimal()
```
**24-hour activity profiles:** 
All three panels share the same daily rhythm. Activity is lowest around 4 a.m. (near zero), rises from about 6 to 8 a.m., stays on roughly 12 to 15 MIMS through the day, and declines after about 8 p.m. toward midnight. Men and women are almost identical in the "less than high school" and "high school equivalent" groups. In the "more than high school" group, women are somewhat more active than men through the daytime and evening. The smooths describe the average pattern, and the individual lines show large variation between people. It has a few very high values that are most visible in the largest group. The education groups also differ in age, so age may account for some of the differences.

# Problem 3
## Clean the dataset
```{r, message=FALSE}
jan2020  <- read_csv("citibike/Jan_2020_Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "January")
july2020 <- read_csv("citibike/July_2020_Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = "2020", month = "July")
jan2024  <- read_csv("citibike/Jan_2024_Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "January")
july2024 <- read_csv("citibike/July_2024_Citi.csv") |>
  mutate(year = "2024", month = "July")
citi <- bind_rows(jan2020, july2020, jan2024, july2024) |>
  clean_names() |>
  mutate(
    year  = factor(year),
    month = factor(month, levels = c("January", "July")),
    weekdays = factor(weekdays,
      levels = c("Monday", "Tuesday", "Wednesday", "Thursday",
                 "Friday", "Saturday", "Sunday")),
    member_casual = factor(member_casual,
      levels = c("member", "casual"), labels = c("Member", "Casual")),
    rideable_type = factor(rideable_type,
      levels = c("classic_bike", "electric_bike"), labels = c("Classic", "Electric"))
  )

dim(citi)
summary(citi$duration)
colSums(is.na(citi))
```

```{r}
glimpse(citi)
```
**Summary of the dataset:**
The cleaned Citi Bike dataset has 99,485 rows and 9 variables. It combines four files that each hold a 1% sample of rides from January 2020, July 2020, January 2024, and July 2024. Each row is one ride, with a unique ride ID, the bike type, the day of the week, ride duration in minutes, start and end station names, and whether the rider is a member or casual. I added year and month and stored the categorical variables as factors, with weekdays ordered Monday to Sunday. The only missing values are in station names, 43 for start stations and 207 for end stations, which is a very small share of the data.

## Total number of rides in each combination of year and month
```{r}
citi |>
  count(year, month, member_casual) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = member_casual, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(Total = Member + Casual) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Year", "Month", "Members", "Casual", "Total"),
        caption = "Number of rides by year, month, and rider type",
        format.args = list(big.mark = ","))
```
**Comments:**
Members account for most rides in every month, but the balance shifts with season. There is a increase from 2024 January to 2024 July. Casual riders are far more seasonal. Their rides rise about 6 times from January to July in 2020 and about 5 times in 2024. Member rides rise a little bit in 2020, about 2 times in 2024. Total rides also grew substantially from 2020 to 2024, by about 52% in January and 124% in July. Since each file is a 1% sample, the counts show relative sizes and not actual ride totals and it is not a full-year trend.

## 5 favorite starting stations
```{r}
citi |>
  filter(year == "2024", month == "July", !is.na(start_station_name)) |>
  count(start_station_name, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 5) |>
  kable(col.names = c("Starting station", "Number of rides"),
        caption = "Five most popular starting stations, July 2024")
```

**Comments:**
The most popular starting stations are all in Manhattan: Pier 61 at Chelsea Piers (163 rides), University Pl & E 14 St (155), W 21 St & 6 Ave (152), West St & Chambers St (150), and W 31 St & 7 Ave (146). The counts are close together, with only 17 rides separating first from fifth.


## Effects of day of the week, month, and year on median ride duration
```{r}
citi |>
  group_by(year, month, weekdays) |>
  summarize(median_duration = median(duration), .groups = "drop") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = weekdays, y = median_duration, color = year, group = year)) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(title = "Median ride duration by day of week, month, and year",
       x = "Day of week", y = "Median duration (minutes)", color = "Year") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

**Comments:**
First, I found out that July rides are longer than January rides in both years, with medians of roughly 13.5 to 16.5 minutes in July 2020 versus 8.5 to 10 in January 2020, and 9 to 11 versus 7.4 to 8.1 in 2024. Second, 2024 rides are shorter than 2020 rides in every weekday and both months, and the gap is much larger in July than in January. Third, weekends tend to have longer rides than weekdays. However, the weekend effect is weak in January 2024, where Sunday is actually among the lowest values. 

## Impact of month, membership status, and bike type on the distribution of ride duration in 2024
```{r}
citi |>
  filter(year == "2024") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = month, y = duration, fill = rideable_type)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ member_casual) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(title = "Ride duration in 2024 by month, membership, and bike type",
       x = "Month", y = "Duration (minutes, log scale)", fill = "Bike type") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Comments:**
Casual riders take longer rides than members in every combination, and their durations are more spread out. Bike type matters differently by group. Among casual riders, electric bikes have shorter median rides than classic bikes in both months. Among members, the two bike types are close, and electric is slightly longer in July. July rides are longer than January rides for almost all groups.
